rows.answer:
Friday deploys are not banned, but they need approval. Under the handbook, deploys to production run Monday through Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific, and Friday deploys require approval from the on-call engineering manager [1][2]. A Friday afternoon push is outside the normal window, so you would need that approval first.

A few other rules apply:

- **Canary bake:** Since October 12, every deploy sits in the canary cell for 45 minutes before it can promote automatically, not 20 [2].
- **Data-plane waves:** Changes under `ingest/` or `runner/` roll out in waves with 30 minutes between each, so they take longer to reach every cell [2].
- **Month-end billing freeze:** Right now there is a freeze on normal changes to Ledger from the last business day of the month until invoices are sent, usually on the 2nd [3]. The last business day of October was Friday, October 30, so this freeze is active today.
- **Rollbacks:** These are allowed at any time, without approval, including during freezes [1][2][3].

If you're shipping a fix during an incident, the incident commander can approve skipping the bake with `/deploy expedite` [2]. Changes that need a normal approval also need sign-off from the owning team's change approver, which for Platform is Oluwaseun Adeyemi (delegate Kofi Mensah) [3][6].

rows.answer:
No. Don't paste a patient's history into a chatbot, even with the name removed.

Halcyon's policy says PHI can only go into AI tools on the approved list, and public chatbots and general-purpose AI assistants are explicitly excluded, including on personal phones [1]. The approved list has three tools, and none of them is a general chatbot [1]:

- **Quillon Ambient:** AI scribe for visit notes. Pilot clinics only (Riverside and Elm Park), with patient verbal consent and clinician sign-off [1].
- **Meridian draft replies:** drafts portal replies inside Meridian EHR. A clinician must edit or approve before sending [1].
- **Halcyon Assist:** internal policy assistant. PHI is not allowed, and it's for policy questions only [1].

Removing the name doesn't make a case non-identifiable. The approved-tools guidance says to treat any patient details as PHI [1]. The HIPAA policy also says PHI must never go into AI tools that aren't approved [2].

If you need a summary of a patient's history, use the EHR (Meridian), which holds the full clinical record [3]. If you think PHI has already gone into an unapproved tool, report it to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours at privacy@halcyon.example or through the compliance hotline [2].

rows.answer:
The Bayline incident involved **17 lab results** filed into the wrong patient's charts at the Riverside and Northgate clinics between July 21 and 23, 2026 [1].

**Why it happened**, per the root cause analysis (RCA-26-07) [1]:

- **Unannounced feed change:** On July 20, Bayline changed its results feed and moved the medical record number (MRN) into a different HL7 segment, without notice [1].
- **Fallback matching:** The interface engine could no longer find the MRN, so it fell back to a secondary rule that matched results on last name and year of birth only. That rule had existed since 2021 and had never been used at volume [1].
- **No monitoring:** Nobody was alerted that 100% of Bayline results were using the fallback rule [1].
- **No contractual notice requirement:** The Bayline agreement did not require advance notice of feed format changes [1].

**Impact and response:** A medical assistant at Riverside spotted a potassium result that didn't match the patient's history on July 23. Two patients had follow-up delayed by four and six days, and neither suffered lasting harm. All 17 results were moved to the correct charts by July 24 [1].

**Corrective actions:** The fallback match was removed and unmatched results now go to a manual queue, and an alert fires when more than 1% of a lab's results use a fallback match in an hour. Both were marked done by September 30 [1]. Two items remained in progress: a 30-day change-notice clause in the lab agreement (due December 31) and a positive patient identification check before results reach the patient portal (due November 30) [1]. The portal check is tracked as project Heron, with a Q4 2026 target [5].

rows.answer:
Halcyon has no exact equivalent of a five-business-day postmortem deadline. Its closest rule is a root cause analysis (RCA) that is due much later: **within 45 calendar days** of the event becoming known [1].

The sentinel event timeline in Halcyon's policy is:

- **Within 1 hour:** the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director [1].
- **Within 24 hours:** anyone involved or who witnessed the event files a report in SafeReport, and the attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family [1].
- **Within 72 hours:** Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) charters the RCA team [1].
- **Within 45 calendar days:** the RCA is completed [1]. Completed RCAs and their action plans then go to the Patient Safety Committee, which meets monthly [1].

The policy applies this RCA requirement to Level 1 (sentinel) and Level 2 (adverse event with harm) events [1]. A sentinel event is defined as patient death or permanent harm not related to the natural course of illness, severe temporary harm, a wrong-patient or wrong-site procedure, or patient suicide within 72 hours of a visit [1].

The Halcyon documents don't use the term "incident commander" for clinic patient incidents. The role that coordinates the immediate response is the **charge nurse** on shift [3].

- **Charge nurse:** coordinates the immediate response to a patient event. This includes assigning who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures the equipment, medications or records involved [3].
- **Clinic manager:** takes over when the clinic has no charge nurse on shift [3]. The staffing standard says a charge nurse is designated in medium and small clinics whenever two or more RNs are on shift; otherwise the clinic manager fills that role [1]. Large clinics have a designated charge nurse [1].
- **On-call medical director:** the charge nurse notifies this person within 1 hour for a sentinel event [3]. The on-call medical director is the senior physician on duty for the whole network [2].

Anyone involved or who witnessed the event must file a report in SafeReport [3]. Level 1 and Level 2 events then get a root cause analysis, and the Patient Safety Committee, chaired by Dr. Kenji Watanabe, reviews the completed analyses [3].

Before a vendor can receive patient data at Halcyon, it needs two things in place: a signed business associate agreement (BAA) and a completed security risk assessment. Halcyon uses the HIPAA term BAA rather than "DPA." The Tallgrass record states that a vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on Halcyon's behalf is a business associate, and that a signed BAA must exist before any PHI is disclosed, including test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [6].

For new AI tools that will handle PHI, Halcyon also requires:
1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed BAA.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO [7].

PHI may only be stored in the EHR, the practice management system, and approved Halcyon systems on the intranet [8].

The vendor register shows the current state. Quillon Ambient has an executed BAA (July 30, 2026) and a completed security risk assessment (July 2026) [5]. Tallgrass Survey Co. has no executed BAA and no PHI may be shared until one is signed; its security assessment passed with conditions in September 2026 [6].

Two gaps to check:
- The business associate table lists a BAA date for Tallgrass (2026-08-05), but the detailed Tallgrass record says the BAA is not executed and the August date is when the draft arrived. Confirm the status with the Privacy Officer before relying on that date [6].
- The table has no BAA date for Brightwater Billing Services or Polyglen Interpreting, so I couldn't confirm their BAA status from the register [1][4].

Yes, but Northwind's version covers a different thing. Northwind has no EHR. Its closest equivalent is emergency access for support engineers to customer workspaces, which is a production-access exception rather than a clinical override [2]. Halcyon's break-the-glass lets a clinician open a patient chart outside their normal treatment relationship [1].

**Halcyon (break-the-glass, Meridian EHR)**
- **Trigger:** An urgent unscheduled patient, covering for a colleague, or an escalation on another clinic's telehealth panel [1].
- **Steps:** Click Emergency access, choose a reason (Emergency care, Coverage, or Other), and write a short justification [1].
- **Duration:** Access lasts until the end of the shift, up to 12 hours [1].
- **Approval:** None in the moment, since patient care comes first [1].
- **Review:** Every event is logged and reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days. Managers may be asked to confirm unclear reasons [1].
- **Misuse:** Inappropriate use is a privacy incident and can lead to sanctions up to termination [1][4].

**Northwind (emergency workspace access)**
- **Trigger:** Only with an open support case or declared incident. Curiosity or convenience isn't a reason [2].
- **Approval:** A second engineer from support or on-call must approve in Teleport. You can't approve your own request, and the approver can't be on the same case [2].
- **Duration:** 2 hours, deliberately shorter than the standard 8-hour production session. Longer access needs a new request [2][3].
- **Access level:** Read-only by default. Write access needs the customer's written consent in the case first [2].
- **Recording and visibility:** Sessions are recorded and kept for one year. The customer's audit log shows the access, and enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours. Security samples sessions weekly, and reviews every session that used write access [2].

**Key differences**
- Halcyon's override is self-service with after-the-fact review. Northwind requires a second person to approve before access starts [1][2].
- Halcyon allows up to 12 hours. Northwind caps emergency access at 2 hours [1][2].
- Northwind tells the customer when access happens. The Halcyon sources don't mention notifying patients [1][2].
- Northwind's default is read-only. The Halcyon sources don't describe read/write limits [1][2].

**No, not for the most sensitive data at either organization.** Each has a clear rule, and the Halcyon rule is stricter.

**Halcyon Health:** Never put PHI in Slack, including DMs. The systems inventory lists Slack as "Never, including DMs" [3]. The HIPAA privacy policy says the same: never put PHI in email subject lines, Slack, personal notes apps, or unapproved AI tools [4]. For PHI sent to outside providers, use encrypted email with `[secure]` in the subject line [3][4].

**Northwind Labs:** Restricted data is never allowed in tickets or Slack. That includes customer event payloads, credentials and encryption keys [2]. Restricted data never leaves production, so use field names and counts instead of pasting payloads [5]. Confidential data (financials, contracts, employee data) is shared only on a need-to-know basis [2]. The policy does not say it is banned from Slack, but sharing should be limited to people who need it [2].

If you see sensitive data where it shouldn't be, report it in `#security-help` (or email security@northwind.example). Good-faith reports are not penalized [2].

rows.answer:
Changing the send time is a significant change, so it needs three approvals, not just one.

1. **System steward: Felix Brandt.** The medication reminder scheduler, Pillbox, is owned by Digital Health Engineering — Patient Engagement (DHE-PE) [5], and Felix Brandt is that team's steward [1].
2. **Clinical safety sign-off: Dr. Anjali Rao, the CMIO**, or her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei [1].
3. **Review at CSCAB**, the weekly Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board, which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [1].

Reminder and outreach automation is named explicitly as significant [1]. Since IR-0412, when duplicate reminders were sent, reminders also carry an idempotency key, and scheduler changes need a written runbook and clinical safety sign-off [3]. If the change moves the job to a different runner or server, the runbook must state how double-running is prevented [1].

The on-call medical director can approve an emergency change only to stop ongoing patient harm, and CSCAB then reviews it at its next meeting [1]. A timing preference does not qualify.

Recent CSCAB practice shows that a clinical safety sign-off can be withheld even after steward approval. On October 28, a patient-facing message was deferred until the delegate's sign-off was given [7]. Plan for that step, and bring the change to CSCAB with the clinical safety case in advance.

The fix would go to **Switchyard**, the in-house interface engine that routed the Bayline results into the wrong charts [2][9]. Because the fix changes result routing, it is a significant change, and it needs three approvals [1]:

1. **System steward: Owen Mbeki**, Integration Services (INT), which owns Switchyard [1][9].
2. **Clinical safety sign-off: Dr. Anjali Rao, CMIO**, or her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei [1].
3. **Review at the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB)**, which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [1].

If the fix were an emergency change to stop ongoing patient harm, the on-call medical director could approve it, and CSCAB would review it at its next meeting [1].

The root cause analysis lists the Switchyard fixes from the incident as already done, including removing the name-and-birth-year fallback match and adding an alert for fallback matches [2]. Two actions were still in progress as of the September review: a 30-day change-notice clause in the Bayline agreement, and a positive patient identification check before results reach the patient portal, owned by Clinical Informatics [2].

Cycle 5 picked three big bets: **Tributary**, **Lantern**, and **Hydrant** [1]. The handbook caps each cycle at three big bets [2].

1. **Tributary:** streaming joins (the Enrich step). Scope was CDC-backed snapshots, the editor preview, dead-letter routing, and a private beta with design partners in October. GA target was January 2027 [1]. The codename register lists it as in private beta since October 1, with GA in January 2027 [4].
2. **Lantern:** a self-serve billing portal where customers manage invoices, plans, payment methods, and usage reports. It depends on the payment-provider migration [1]. Its timeline has changed. The pitch targeted beta in December and GA in January 2027 [1]. Later leadership notes moved GA to March 2027 and beta to February [5], and the codename register agrees [4].
3. **Hydrant:** automatic scaling of ingest gateways per cell. It shipped to all production cells on October 22, 2026 [3][4].

An Enterprise workspace is specified for reference tables of up to **500 million rows** per workspace [3]. That figure comes from a product spec, so treat it as the target rather than a confirmed shipped limit. The spec is also tied to the streaming joins feature, which was in private beta in October with GA targeted for January 2027 [4].

Two related points:

- The spec sets the Growth plan limit at 50 million rows [3].
- Snapshot rebuilds get slow at large sizes. A 50M-row table takes about 25 minutes to rebuild after a runner restart, which is why RFC-031 proposes persisting snapshots [2]. That RFC was still pending a security sign-off, and nothing ships to the beta until it's approved [2].

I didn't find a separate published limit for Enterprise reference tables, so confirm the 500M figure with the product or account team before quoting it to a customer.

rows.answer:
When a customer exceeds their limit, the API returns **HTTP 429**, and the response includes a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait [1]. The SDKs honour that header automatically and back off exponentially, so customers using them generally don't need to build their own retry logic [1].

**Key details:**

- **Scope:** Limits are per workspace, not per API key. Ten keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- **Bursts:** Short bursts of up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- **Quota:** Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].
- **Not a 429:** Endpoints that a customer's plan doesn't include return HTTP 403, not 429 [1].

**Per-endpoint limits** vary by plan. For example, event ingest (`POST /v2/events`) is 100 req/s on Starter, 2,000 req/s on Growth, and 10,000 req/s on Enterprise, while triggering a pipeline run (`POST /v2/pipelines/{id}/runs`) is 1, 10, and 25 req/s on those plans [1]. The full table is in the rate limits page [1].

Don't confuse this with HTTP 503 responses. Those come from outages, not rate limiting. During the August 2026 ingest outage, rejected events were returned with 503 and retried by customer SDKs [3].

**Where to ask:** Request a new codename in `#eng-leads` [1].

**Naming rules:**
- **Internal only.** Codenames must never appear in customer-facing material, release notes, or the status page [1].
- **No collisions.** A new codename must not match a production service name, a vendor name, or an existing codename [1]. For example, Sandbar (the EU cell project) is not Saltmarsh, which is a vendor [1].
- **Informal service nicknames aren't codenames.** Terms like "the firehose" (`ingest-gateway`) or "the till" (Ledger) are informal names for production services [1].
- **Use real service names in durable documents.** Runbooks, postmortems, and tickets should use the real service name, not a codename or nickname [1].

Mateo Alvarez (Group PM) maintains the codename register, which was last updated October 28, 2026 [1]. Before you ask, check the register so you don't duplicate one of the eight existing codenames [1].

You need sign-off from **Oluwaseun Adeyemi**, PLAT's change approver. Their delegate is **Kofi Mensah** [6]. Raising a gateway ceiling is a normal change under the production change approval policy [2][3].

- **Why PLAT:** Hydrant is owned by PLAT, and the gateways it scales are owned by DP. Each cell's floor and ceiling live in the PLAT infrastructure repo [1][3].
- **No security sign-off needed:** Hydrant stores no customer data and is not a Restricted service [3].
- **The ceiling for us-east:** it is currently 16 / 64 (floor / ceiling) [2].
- **Requests go to:** the PLAT channel, `#team-platform` [3][6].

A temporary hold doesn't need approval, but it can't raise the ceiling. `nwctl hydrant hold` pins a cell's replica count for at most 4 hours, then Hydrant takes over again [3]. Use it only as a stopgap while the ceiling change is pending.

Also note that Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call when a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, because that usually points to a gateway problem rather than real traffic [3]. Before you raise the ceiling, check whether the us-east pinning reflects real load or a gateway fault.

- **runner**: executes customer pipelines. It stores partition state in local RocksDB and reference-table snapshots. Owner: DP [1].

A deploy sits in the canary cell for **45 minutes** before it can be promoted automatically [1]. This replaces the 20 minutes in the Engineering Handbook. The October 2026 pipeline note says it applies wherever the two differ, and the handbook will be updated to match [1][2]. The longer bake was added because INC-2291 showed that some failures only appear after caches or sessions expire [1].

Promotion also needs to pass these checks during the bake:
- Error rate and p95 latency stay within 10% of the baseline (unchanged) [1].
- No sustained TLS handshake errors between gateways and brokers in canary [1].
- Runner consumer lag does not grow by more than 2 minutes during the bake [1].

A few related points:
- Anyone can run `/deploy hold <deploy-id>` in Slack to keep a deploy in canary. It stays there until someone runs `/deploy release` or rolls it back [1].
- `nwctl deploy status` shows where each deploy is, which checks it has passed, and how long until the next wave [1].
- The incident commander can skip the bake with `/deploy expedite`, and the expedite is logged in `#eng-changes` [1].
- Data-plane changes (under `ingest/` or `runner/`) roll out in waves after canary, with 30 minutes between waves [1].

**No. Don't run `nwctl scale ingest` by hand for us-west.** The runbook still lists that step, but it's out of date. Hydrant, the gateway autoscaler, has replaced it and is live in us-west (enabled October 15) [3]. The launch notes say Hydrant will revert a manual change within 2 minutes [3].

**What to do instead:**

- **Check Hydrant first.** It scales up when average gateway CPU stays above 65% for 3 minutes, adding 25% of current replicas (at least 2) per step [3]. At 80%+ CPU it should already be scaling. us-west's floor is 10 replicas and its ceiling is 48 [2].
- **Check the other runbook steps.** The launch notes say to check which cell is affected and look at gateway TLS handshake errors first [3]. INC-2291, the August us-east outage, was a TLS handshake failure cascade [5].
- **If you need to pin the count** (for example, while debugging a bad gateway build), use a hold: `nwctl hydrant hold --cell us-west --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`. Holds last at most 4 hours and need no approval. Release early with `nwctl hydrant release --cell us-west` [3].
- **If it hits the ceiling:** after 10 minutes at the ceiling, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call [3]. Ceiling hits usually mean a gateway problem rather than real traffic [3].

If the 5xx rate stays above 1% and Hydrant is at its ceiling, that's a SEV-2 or worse. Declare the incident with `/incident declare` in Slack [1][3].

The v1 standard also said Enterprise customers may contract for a shorter archive period [1], and I didn't find a v2 statement that confirms this still applies.

An Enterprise workspace can force a reference-table snapshot rebuild once every 2 minutes through the API. The endpoint is `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh`, and the limit is listed as "1 per 2 minutes" for Enterprise (default) [1].

Some related details:
- Limits apply per workspace, not per API key, so all keys in one workspace share the same budget [1].
- If you go over the limit, the API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header. Growth is limited to 1 per 10 minutes, and Starter cannot use this endpoint at all (it returns HTTP 403) [1].
- Forced rebuilds are expensive because they discard the runner's snapshot and rescan the full table. Snapshots are normally kept current with change data capture, so most customers never need to force one [1].

rows.answer:
No, don't throw the vaccines out yet. The formulary's cold-chain procedure says to keep them and get a pharmacist's decision first. Vaccine refrigerators must stay between 2 °C and 8 °C, so 10 °C is out of range [1].

What to do now:

1. **Don't discard anything.** Label the affected stock "Do not use." Move it to a working refrigerator and keep it cold. Record the reading, the time, and how long it has been out of range [1].
2. **Call the clinical pharmacist within 1 hour.** The pharmacist checks with the manufacturers whether the stock can still be used [1].
3. **File a SafeReport.** If no vaccine was given, it is a Level 4 near miss. If a patient received affected vaccine, the level is higher [1][2].
4. **Don't give any vaccine from the affected stock** until the clinical pharmacist releases it in writing [1].

Frozen vaccines are never refrozen or reused once thawed [1].

The knowledge base doesn't say how long the fridge has been at 10 °C, so the pharmacist's answer will decide whether the stock is usable. If you're not sure who the clinical pharmacist is on duty, your clinic manager can help.

**Short answer:** Keep trying the ordering clinician for up to 30 minutes. If you still haven't reached them, the result goes to the on-call medical director. For Wednesday, November 18, that is Dr. Luis Carvalho, with Dr. Ingrid Solberg as backup.

**Timing**
- Critical results must reach the ordering clinician within 60 minutes. If the ordering clinician can't be reached within 30 minutes, the result goes to the on-call medical director [1].
- Document each notification in the chart with the time and the person notified [1].

**Who to call on November 18**
- Week 47 runs November 16–23. The on-call medical director is Dr. Luis Carvalho, and the backup is Dr. Ingrid Solberg [2].
- Reach them through the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144, option 2. The service pages the on-call director and, if there is no callback within 10 minutes, pages the backup [2].
- Don't text physicians' personal mobile numbers. Pages through the answering service are logged and timed, which the chart documentation needs [2].

**Caveat:** The protocol I found sets the 30-minute point for escalation but doesn't say how long to keep trying before that. I didn't find a separate policy covering this, so check with your clinic's supervising physician if you need more detail.

**Other details to confirm:**
- RZV is for patients aged 50 and over. The second dose is due 2–6 months after the first [1].
- RZV must be given by an RN or clinician [1].

Halcyon no longer charges a fee for missed appointments. The no-show fee was eliminated by the revised policy effective October 5, 2026 [1]. The policy says Halcyon no longer charges patients for missed appointments, and any unpaid no-show fees billed before October 5, 2026 are waived. Revenue Cycle Management will reverse them, and front desk staff should not try to collect them [1].

The old 2025 policy charged a $25 fee after a second no-show in 12 months, with 24 hours' notice needed to avoid a no-show [2]. That no longer applies.

Under the current policy, a missed appointment counts as a no-show if the patient did not cancel at least 2 hours ahead, and cancelling by replying to a reminder counts [1]. Instead of charging, the policy focuses on barriers. After a third no-show in 12 months, a care coordinator calls the patient to offer help such as ride vouchers or a telehealth visit [1]. Patients are not discharged for no-shows [1].

A patient who arrives **more than 10 minutes** after their appointment time must be offered the next open slot that day with any clinician, or be rescheduled. This is the current rule, from the policy revised in October 2026 and effective October 5, 2026 [3].

The front desk isn't required to act on arrivals within 10 minutes. The clinician may still see a patient who is more than 10 minutes late if the schedule allows [3].

The older 2025 policy used a 15-minute threshold [2], so that figure no longer applies. Patients who are late because of an interpreter or accessibility issue on Halcyon's side are never rescheduled for being late [3].

No. Under the current staffing standard, every clinic, including small clinics, must have at least one RN on site during open hours. Saturday sessions also need an RN [2]. The Sunday session at Harbor Point also lists 1 RN on site [2].

The standard that allowed small clinics to run without an RN was the 2025 version, and it has been replaced [1][2]. The revision followed a Q2 2026 review that found small clinics without an RN were sending too many triage calls to the physician [2].

If an RN is missing, the rules still apply in other ways. Every clinic must have at least one physician or NP on site during open hours. If coverage drops below that, the clinic manager contacts the float pool first, then converts in-person visits to telehealth where clinically appropriate [2][3]. The float pool is also required to have 2 RNs on call daily [2]. I did not find a rule for a clinic running a session with no RN and no float cover. The 2025 standard suggested the clinic manager ask the regional medical director about reducing the schedule, but that document is superseded [1].

rows.answer:
Patient safety events at Halcyon are logged in **SafeReport**. Anyone involved in or who witnessed the event files the report, and the policy says reporting is never optional and never punished [1].

**Who does what, and when**

- **Immediately:** Make the patient safe and follow the clinical escalation protocol, calling 911 if needed. Tell the charge nurse on shift. If the clinic has no charge nurse on shift, tell the clinic manager [1].
- **Sentinel events:** The charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour [1]. To reach the on-call director, call the answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2 [3].
- **Filing the report:** Anyone involved or who witnessed the event files in SafeReport [1]. The excerpt I found gives no explicit deadline for filing, although the policy section that lists these steps is headed "Within 24 hours" [1]. Check with your Quality & Patient Safety team if you need a firm filing deadline.
- **Disclosure:** The attending clinician tells the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1].
- **Follow-up:** Level 1 and Level 2 events get a root cause analysis. QPS charters the team within 72 hours, and the RCA must be completed within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1].

**Event levels**

Level 1 is a sentinel event, Level 2 is an adverse event with harm, Level 3 is a no-harm event, and Level 4 is a near miss [1]. Near misses are also logged in SafeReport when a session runs without an RN [2].

**Related reporting**

- Privacy incidents, such as a misdirected fax or a lost device, go to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours at privacy@halcyon.example or through the compliance hotline [4]. They are handled separately from patient safety events [1].

Northwind's approach is close to a just-culture model, though it uses the term "blameless." Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 gets a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution. The postmortem looks at the system and the process rather than individuals, and names appear only in the timeline [2]. Postmortems are reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [2].

The incident commander (IC) picks the author, usually the responder who knew the most about the failure [2]. The IC coordinates the incident and doesn't debug it, so the author is typically an engineer from the responding team rather than the IC [2].

For example, the August 14 ingest outage (INC-2291, SEV-1) was written by Priya Raman with the ingest team, even though the IC on the incident log was Oluwaseun Adeyemi [1][3].

Current status: the INC-2351 postmortem draft was circulated on October 21 and is due for review at the November 5 reliability meeting [1].

**Short answer:** Halcyon's documents describe a monthly review of EHR access logs, but I found no periodic check that asks whether each person still needs their access. I also found no rule for what happens if nobody signs off. Northwind Labs does have a quarterly access review with automatic revocation, but that policy covers Northwind's own systems, not Halcyon's EHR.

**What Halcyon documents say**
- The compliance team reviews EHR access logs monthly using automated anomaly detection. Unusual access triggers a review with the employee's manager [1].
- Clinical system access is suspended automatically if HIPAA training is more than 14 days overdue [1].
- Break-the-glass access is logged and reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days. If the reason is unclear, the manager is asked to confirm it [3].

**What Northwind documents say (not the EHR)**
- Quarterly access reviews are run by each team lead. Access that is not re-confirmed is revoked automatically [2].
- Exceptions need written approval from the Head of Security and expire after 90 days [2].

**Gap to check:** If your compliance team needs a documented recertification step for Meridian EHR access, the knowledge base doesn't show one. Ask the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway, per [3]) or the HIPAA Security Officer whether one exists outside these documents.

**Halcyon (patient data):** Before any staff use a new AI tool with PHI, the tool must be on Halcyon's approved list, and the tool needs four things [1]:

The knowledge base doesn't give a typical turnaround for this review. Recent Northwind reviews are logged with a `#vendor-review` ticket and a result such as "Passed" or "Conditional pass" [5][6][8][10].

Note that the Halcyon requirements apply to Halcyon staff and don't govern Northwind's review. If you're working on a Halcyon tool, the BAA step is usually the bottleneck.

The Halcyon equivalent is the **system steward** for the owning team. The Halcyon app is owned by Digital Health Engineering — Patient Engagement (DHE-PE), and that team's steward is **Felix Brandt** [1][3].

Their approval is enough on its own, as long as the change stays minor. Cosmetic changes are "minor" and need steward approval only [1]. Significant changes are different. They need the steward, plus clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO, Dr. Anjali Rao (or her delegate, Dr. Benedict Osei), plus review at CSCAB [1]. Significant changes cover patient-facing automation, the patient app's clinical content, medication information, and similar areas [1].

A purely cosmetic change to the bill-pay screen should qualify as minor, since bill pay isn't clinical content. Two checks before you rely on that:
- If the tweak touches anything beyond appearance, such as wording that triggers messages, routing, or clinical content, it may become significant.
- The minor/significant call is set by the policy, so if you're unsure, confirm with Felix Brandt or the CMIO's office.

rows.answer:
**Northwind Labs (October duplicate invoices, INC-2340):** The fix is an idempotency key on invoice creation, scoped to each workspace and billing period, so a second run can't create a second invoice for the same period. It shipped October 8 [10]. The root cause was that a payment-provider webhook timed out, the retry re-ran the batch, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent [8]. The team also added a daily reconciliation report comparing invoices with charges, which is marked done [10]. An alert for webhook timeouts during billing batches is still open, due November 6 [10].

**Halcyon Health (September duplicate medication reminders, IR-0412):** The fix is an idempotency key on each reminder, built from patient, medication and scheduled time. A reminder whose key already exists is never sent again [1]. The cause was a September 2 move to a new job runner: the old and new runners both ran during cutover, and neither checked whether a reminder had already gone out [1]. Halcyon also made two process changes. Scheduler cutovers now require a written runbook and clinical safety sign-off [1], and that runbook must state how double-running is prevented [2]. The Marigold refill-acknowledgement project is applying the same idempotency-key rule [3].

One thing to note: the Northwind Slack export says the fix was merged and deployed on October 6 [8], while the status tracker gives October 8 as the ship date [10]. Both are in the sources, so you may want to confirm the exact date before quoting it to your client.

**Northwind Labs has a holiday change freeze. Halcyon Health does not have an IT freeze.**

**Northwind Labs**
- **Holiday freeze: December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027.** Only standard and emergency changes ship during this window [4]. The on-call rota describes the week of December 22 as inside the freeze and expects a quiet week [1].
- **Month-end billing freeze:** no normal changes to Ledger from the last business day of the month until invoices are sent, usually the 2nd [4]. This is already active: the freeze started Friday, October 30, and runs until invoices go out, expected around November 2 [7].

- Billing and identity work is also affected. The Undertow cutover is set for January 19, 2027, after the holiday freeze [7].

**Halcyon Health**
- There is no IT freeze. The October Juniper steering committee notes say so directly [6].
- Clinic managers asked that Juniper pilot training not fall in the week of December 21 [6]. The pilot go/no-go meeting is December 16 [6].
- Clinical system changes still need approval from the owning team's system steward under the clinical systems change control policy [5].

For planning, Northwind's freeze covers the December 18 to January 4 window. Only standard and emergency changes are allowed, so plan any normal changes before December 18 or after January 4.

**Err high.** At both companies, if you can't tell how serious something is, rate it at the higher level. Downgrading later is easy.

- **Northwind (incidents, SEV levels):** "When unsure, declare higher; downgrading is cheap." [3] The person who declares the incident picks the initial severity, and the incident commander (IC) can raise or lower it at any time. [3] The runbook defines SEV-1 as data loss or a full ingest or pipeline outage for a cell, and SEV-2 as a partial outage or degradation affecting many customers. [1]
- **Halcyon (patient safety events):** "When unsure, report at the higher level." [2] Levels run from 1 (sentinel event) down to 4 (near miss). [2] The Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) team reclassifies events if needed. [2] The policy is owned by Quality & Patient Safety and was approved by the Patient Safety Committee. [2]

So the initial rating can be set by whoever declares or reports it, but the later change is made by the Northwind IC at any point during an incident [3], or by QPS for Halcyon events [2]. The sources don't name a specific person for the Halcyon reclassification.

**Halcyon's patient survey vendor (Tallgrass Survey Co.)** is held up by a retention dispute. Tallgrass is proposing a business associate agreement (BAA), not a data processing agreement. Tallgrass wants to keep identifiable survey responses for 5 years for benchmarking, while Halcyon will accept 18 months [10]. The security risk assessment was completed in September 2026 and passed with conditions. The signed order form is on hold until the BAA is executed [10]. The Privacy Officer, Margaret Holloway, is due to send revised retention language by November 6, 2026 [10].

Until the BAA is signed, no PHI may be shared with Tallgrass, including for pilots or test files. Juniper patients get the in-app survey instead [10][11].

**Halcyon offers the bigger discount: 20% versus Northwind's 15%.** The two aren't directly comparable, though, because they apply to different things.

- **Northwind:** Annual prepayment on the Growth plan earns a 15% discount, equivalent to $12,240 per year off the $1,200/month list price [6]. A September 2026 sales memo confirms the 15% prepayment discount is unchanged for quotes from October 1, 2026 [7].
- **Halcyon:** Self-pay patients who pay in full on the day of service get a 20% prompt-pay discount [2]. This applies to visits, such as the $165 new-patient or $120 established-patient self-pay rates [2]. It does not apply to vaccines and injectables, which are already priced at cost plus administration [1].

So for a self-pay patient paying a visit in full on the day, Halcyon's 20% is the larger discount. For a vaccine or injectable, Halcyon gives no prompt-pay discount at all.

**Northwind Labs:** During a declared incident, the **incident commander (IC)** can approve an emergency change, including one that would normally need the owning team's change approver [3][4]. The current IC rotation is Kofi Mensah, Priya Raman, Harriet Vance, Oluwaseun Adeyemi and Ravi Subramanian [1]. The IC is paged by `/incident declare` [4].

Review afterwards:
- The owning team's change approver must review the emergency change retroactively within two business days [3].
- Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 incident gets a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution, reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [4].

**Halcyon Health:** The **on-call medical director** may approve an emergency change to a clinical system, but only to stop ongoing patient harm [2]. The on-call medical director is the senior physician on duty for the whole network, and the November rota says they may approve emergency changes to clinical systems [5]. To reach them, call the answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2 [5].

Review afterwards: the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) reviews the change at its next meeting [2]. CSCAB meets weekly on Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [2]. The documents I found don't set a deadline for this review, and I didn't find a separate post-change review step for Halcyon.

I didn't check who is on call this weekend. The November rota is the one I found, and it doesn't cover today's date.
